claims.text: The initial material consists of nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a homogeneous, single-phase structure at room temperature.
Atomic-scale thermal behavior can be investigated by in-situ heating in an aberration-corrected TEM.
The in-situ TEM experiment can be conducted at elevated temperature under a controlled environment such as high vacuum.
Atomic-scale lattice sites and interfaces may serve as nucleation points for segregation or ordering transitions.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermodynamic fluctuations mediate the enhanced atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility triggers local structural rearrangements.
Local structural rearrangements lead to segregation or ordering phenomena.
Heating will produce atomic-scale structural changes such as local compositional segregation or ordering.
Segregation or ordering can be directly imaged at atomic resolution in the proposed TEM experiment.
Heating may cause distinct phases or local-composition variations to emerge relative to the initial homogeneous state.
Detection of these changes would support the proposition that thermodynamic contributions influence nanoparticle structure at high temperature.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles have a uniform atomic arrangement at room temperature.
The method is limited to nanoparticles small enough for TEM imaging.
Sintering or melting would prevent meaningful atomic-scale assessment under the proposed conditions.
The temperature threshold for the onset of structural changes is unknown.
Whether the structural evolution is gradual or abrupt is unknown.
Absence of discernible segregation, ordering, defect formation, or other atomic-scale changes after heating would falsify the proposed measurable structural evolution.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis states categorically that segregation or ordering will occur, whereas the predicted outcome treats such changes as conditional ('if detected').
